name: Renal Tubular Acidosis Type 4

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Type 4 Renal Tubular Acidosis Diagnostic Criteria

criteria.description: Persistent hyperkalemia (serum potassium >5.0 mmol/L) without other causes
Presence of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
Evidence of hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance (low plasma aldosterone or impaired response)
Impaired urinary acidification with urine pH typically <5.5
Exclusion of other causes of hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of persistent hyperkalemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with evidence of hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes of hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis such as chronic kidney disease or medications.

pathognomonic.notes: Elevated serum potassium levels due to impaired renal potassium excretion
Metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap caused by impaired acid secretion

common.notes: Due to hyperkalemia affecting neuromuscular function
Generalized tiredness related to electrolyte imbalance
Increased urine output secondary to tubular dysfunction
May be present due to underlying aldosterone abnormalities

occasional.notes: Resulting from hyperkalemia affecting cardiac conduction
Loss of appetite related to electrolyte disturbances
Due to polyuria and electrolyte imbalance

rare.notes: Severe hyperkalemia can cause flaccid paralysis
Rare neurological complication due to severe acidosis

laboratory: Low plasma aldosterone or impaired aldosterone response
Elevated serum creatinine if associated with chronic kidney disease
imaging: Renal ultrasound may show normal or small kidneys if chronic kidney disease present
genetic: Mutations in genes affecting aldosterone synthesis or response (e.g., NR3C2, WNK1/4) in inherited forms
other: Electrocardiogram changes consistent with hyperkalemia (peaked T waves, widened QRS)

distinguishingFeatures: Often accompanied by other signs of renal failure

redFlags: Severe hyperkalemia (>6.5 mmol/L) with ECG changes
Rapid onset muscle weakness or paralysis
references: Kraut JA, Kurtz I. Renal tubular acidosis. N Engl J Med. 2005;352(1):54-64.
Batlle D, Arruda JA. Renal tubular acidosis: diagnosis and treatment. Am J Kidney Dis. 1999;34(5):954-980.
Sterns RH. Disorders of plasma potassium. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(18):1544-1555.
